title: Where the returners stand (Berakhot 34b)
hookLine: where those who have returned stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot
tomorrow: is eating an apple without a word a kind of taking?

cards: Screenshots last forever. Someone changes, really changes, and the group chat still has the receipts from who they used to be. Every time they do something good, somebody scrolls up.
So who stands where even the perfectly good can't? The Talmud's answer is a surprise. Rabbi Abbahu says: in the place where those who return stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand.
The person with the receipts gets the higher ground.

teach.b: The returners have a name in Hebrew: baalei teshuvah, people of return. Teshuvah means turning back, to God and to who you were meant to be.

teach.h: PEACE TO THE FAR, THEN THE NEAR.
teach.b: Rabbi Abbahu finds his proof in a line from Isaiah: peace, peace, to the one who is far and to the one who is near. Far comes first. The one who was far away and came back is greeted before the one who never left.
Then the Talmud does what it does: someone disagrees.
Rabbi Yochanan reads it differently, and says the prophets' promises were spoken for the returners, while what waits for the completely righteous is something no eye has seen.
So the sages argue about the ranking, and neither of them looks down on the person who came back. That matters this week, not in heaven.

teach.h: DON'T SAY: REMEMBER WHAT YOU DID.
teach.b: Elsewhere the Mishnah makes it law: you may not say to someone who has returned, remember what you used to do.

Scrolling up is the very thing it rules out. Here's a way to hear Rabbi Abbahu: the one who never fell hasn't had to climb. The returner knows exactly what pulls, and turned anyway, maybe more than once.

how: Jews call someone who has come back to God and to Jewish life a baal teshuvah, and Jewish law, from the Mishnah on, forbids reminding a returner of their past.

games.q: what does “where the returners stand” mean?
o: people who turned back to God, standing higher than the righteous
the righteous, who stand above everyone who has ever sinned
a place in the synagogue kept for people who arrive late

games.q: the place and the people — tap the pairs.
p: returners stand where the righteous can't
peace to the far and the near
the far one is greeted first
don't say: remember what you used to do

s: in the Talmud, someone who sinned and returned is second-class
Rabbi Abbahu puts them where even the completely righteous can't stand.
every sage on the page agrees with Rabbi Abbahu
Rabbi Yochanan reads it differently, and neither looks down on the returner.
Jewish law forbids reminding a returner of their past
the Mishnah: don't say to them, remember your earlier deeds.

games.q: your cousin was in trouble a lot in middle school. now she volunteers every weekend. at a family dinner, an uncle says, "let's see how long this lasts." what does today's page say?
o: he's being careful; it's fair to wait and see before trusting the change.
she stands somewhere high now, and bringing up the past is ruled out.
she's doing well, but she can't stand as high as someone who never slipped.
games.why: Rabbi Abbahu puts the returner where even the completely righteous can't stand, and the Mishnah forbids saying, remember what you used to do.

practice: Think of one person who has truly changed: a friend, a parent, maybe you. With a pen, write one sentence about who they are now, with nothing about who they used to be.
Read it back slowly, and let it be the whole story for these two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Where the returners stand: Rabbi Abbahu's place, higher than the completely righteous, because the far one is greeted first.

orig.note: Hebrew: people of return; teshuvah means turning back.

carryVoice: A line to keep: returners stand higher, and nobody gets to scroll up on them. Thirty of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (Rabbi Abbahu: where returners stand, the completely righteous cannot; Rabbi Yochanan's differing view)
Isaiah 57:19 (peace, peace, to him that is far off and to him that is near)
Isaiah 64:3 (no eye has seen; cited by Rabbi Yochanan for the completely righteous)
Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 (one may not say to a penitent, remember your former deeds)
